items.title: SHIELD-Net: A Sperm Halo Image Classification Framework via Hybrid ROI Extraction and ROI-Guided Dual-View Learning
items.abstract: The sperm chromatin dispersion (SCD) test is widely used to assess sperm DNA fragmentation by observing the halo structure around the sperm head. However, manual halo interpretation is labor-intensive and subjective, which limits its consistency and throughput in clinical practice. To address these limitations, we propose SHIELD-Net, an image-level single-sperm halo morphology classification framework for four halo categories: large halo, medium halo, small halo, and without halo. SHIELD-Net includes two modules, i.e., a hybrid ROI extraction (HyREx) module and dual-view learning with ROI-guided gate fusion (RGF). The HyREx module converts the traditional direct classification pipeline into a segmentation-classification pipeline. It uses the cell segmentation foundation model, i.e., Cellpose, to segment halo-centered regions of interest (ROIs) and proposes a fallback mechanism to ensure segmentation effectiveness. In this way, HyREx can construct a head–halo-centered ROI and reduce interference from tail and background regions. Based on the original image and the extracted ROI, SHIELD-Net performs dual-view ConvNeXt encoding. RGF further uses the ROI representation to generate a spatial gate that recalibrates the original-view feature map toward halo-morphology-related responses. Experiments were conducted on a public expert-annotated sperm microscopy dataset containing 403 individual sperm halo images using stratified five-fold cross-validation. SHIELD-Net achieved a Macro F1 of 0.9290 ± 0.0161. Compared with the original-image ConvNeXt-Small baseline, SHIELD-Net improved Macro F1 by 0.1755. These results indicate that combining head–halo-centered ROI construction with ROI-guided feature recalibration improves image-level sperm halo morphology classification.

items.title: Should there be a teacher in-the-loop? A study of generative AI-personalized tasks middle school
items.abstract: Abstract Large language models can be used to design instructional tasks to align to students’ needs. These generative AI models can create tasks that correspond to students’ out-of-school interests in areas like sports or music, which may enhance students’ interest in learning. However, little is known about teachers’ processes for creating or modifying tasks with generative AI, despite commercial AI companies’ claims that they will save teachers time. In the present study, 7 middle school mathematics teachers used ChatGPT to create personalized versions of problems in their curriculum to correspond to their students’ interests. The prompting moves teachers made and their students’ open-ended feedback on personalized problems were examined through thematic analysis. Teachers’ efficiency when creating problems and the ratings of their 7th grade students who received personalized assignments were examined. Results from this sample suggest that having a teacher-in-the-loop may result in generative AI-enhanced personalization being enacted at a broad grain size, whereas students often expressed preference for a smaller grain-size where they receive specific popular culture references that interest them. Teachers used prompting to adjust popular culture references and address issues with the depth, ethics, or realism of the problems generated, in some cases showing epistemic agency. The article closes with an exploratory, design-focused look at scalability trade-offs with teacher-facing personalization, patterns of teacher prompting practices, and opportunities for teachers to exercise epistemic and ethical monitoring of personalization outputs.

items.abstract: Skin cancer is among the most prevalent cancers in the world, and early detection of melanoma is the best strategy to lower the associated mortality. Computer-aided diagnosis of skin lesions evolved from hand-crafted feature pipelines based on the ABCD rule and texture descriptors into deep neural networks achieving dermatologists' performance on benchmark-controlled tasks. In this review, we provide a full overview of the automated skin lesion classification pipeline: from the clinical background, over public skin lesion image datasets and challenges, and the early approach of hand-crafted computer vision descriptors over modern state-of-the-art deep learning architectures, vision transformers, self-supervised, and foundation models, multimodal skin lesion analysis explainability uncertainty estimation, down to reader studies or other comparative analyses between algorithms and clinicians. We provide a critical reflection on how far benchmark performance is from translational readiness, and address problems of dataset bias and under-representation of skin types; spurious correlations and artefacts; class imbalance; domain shift; reporting quality; privacy; and regulation. Finally, we conclude with a shared vision for future research in the field of skin cancer detection including the curation of human-labelled representative datasets; use of prospective validation studies; human-AI partnership systems; private training data; and responsible, explainable models. This is a narrative review article and not a systematic review and meta-analysis. We have described results of articles at the study level, and note that differences across performance metrics should be put into context of differences across datasets, reference tasks, and validation approaches.

items.title: Small Language Models for Automated Software Bug Report Classification and Summarization
items.abstract: Before a bug report can be assigned to anyone, somebody has to decide what kind of problem it describes, how serious it is, how soon it needs attention and which component it touches. In busy projects this triage work piles up, and two people reading the same report often disagree. Large Language Models (LLMs) classify text well, but they are costly to run and awkward to deploy for everyday triage. Small Language Models (SLMs) need far less hardware, yet nobody has shown that they cope with the noisy, code-filled text of real bug reports. This paper reviews ten recent studies and proposes a design in which an SLM suggests labels and a short summary, a rule-based layer checks them, and reports the model is unsure about go to a human triager. We also set out how the design should be evaluated. Nothing has been implemented, so the paper makes no claim about accuracy or speed.

items.title: Smart Democracy: Leveraging Artificial Intelligence to Combat Election Misinformation in Nigeria
items.abstract: The increasing use of digital communication technologies has transformed democratic participation in Nigeria, but it has also accelerated the spread of election misinformation through social media and other online platforms. False political information, manipulated digital content, and coordinated disinformation campaigns have continued to undermine electoral credibility, public trust, and informed voter decision-making. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising tool for detecting misinformation, verifying online content, identifying coordinated inauthentic behavior, and supporting evidence-based electoral communication. Despite these opportunities, there is limited empirical evidence on how AI can be effectively integrated into Nigeria's electoral communication system to strengthen democratic governance. This study examines the role of AI in combating election misinformation and promoting smart democracy in Nigeria. Specifically, it investigates the prevalence and patterns of election misinformation, assesses stakeholders' awareness and adoption of AI technologies for misinformation detection, examines the opportunities and challenges associated with AI deployment, and proposes communication strategies for responsible AI use during elections. The study adopts a mixed-methods research design, combining quantitative surveys with qualitative interviews involving electoral officials, journalists, fact-checkers, communication experts, and registered voters. Quantitative data will be analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics, while qualitative data will be analyzed through thematic analysis. The findings are expected to provide practical recommendations for policymakers, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), media organizations, technology developers, and civil society organizations on leveraging AI to enhance electoral transparency, improve information integrity, strengthen public trust, and promote democratic participation in Nigeria. The study contributes to the growing literature on artificial intelligence, development communication, digital governance, and democratic innovation in Africa.

items.title: Smart Digital Twin: An interactive AI Campus Plateform
items.abstract: With the expansion of smart campus technologies, there is now an increasing demand for intelligent and interactive platforms that can make navigating and managing college campuses easier, faster, and more intuitive. In this paper, we present Smart Digital Twin: An Interactive AI Campus Platform, which is an online, digital representation of a campus that incorporates interactive 3D visualization, artificial intelligence, smart navigation, and campus services, The system allows users to explore college buildings and facilities within a virtual environment, receive assistance from an AI assistant through text and voice interaction, and find their way to classrooms, laboratories, and other services thanks to smart indoor and outdoor navigation, The architecture of the platform consists of a React frontend, a Node.js and Express backend, AI services provided via the OpenAI GPT API, MongoDB Atlas for storing data, and mapping services like Mapbox or Leaflet. It uses JSON Web Tokens (JWT) for authentization and offers cloud storage and media services for deploying the platform. This system provides a comprehensive solution by bringing together campus visualization, AI assistant services, navigation and information, aiming to minimize fragmented information access, manual inquiries, facilitate wayfinding, and enhance the overall campus experience. Moreover, its modularity allows for the future integration of IoT data, live occupancy information, smart classrooms, multilingual features, predictive analytics, and emergency workflows.

items.title: Source Expertise, Argument Strength, and Multidimensional Source Sensitivity in Large Language Model Evaluation
items.abstract: Abstract Large language models are increasingly used to evaluate arguments, responses, and decisions, yet their judgments may be influenced by contextual information about who produced the content. This study examined how source expertise relevance and argument strength affect LLM evaluation and whether source effects differ across judgment dimensions. Twenty arguments spanning 10 topics were constructed as strong–weak pairs and presented under four source conditions: relevant expert, irrelevant expert, non-expert, and no source. Four large language models evaluated each argument on logical quality, credibility, persuasiveness, and agreement. Five repetitions were collected for each model-by-argument-by-source-by-dimension combination and averaged before inferential testing. Human validation assessed the intended argument-strength manipulation but showed negligible overall strong–weak separation in the second validation round, including two reversed topic pairs. Separate manipulation checks indicated that the models rated topic-relevant expertise and general professional expertise differently across source conditions. Source attribution most consistently affected credibility. Topic-level robustness analyses showed significant source-condition effects on credibility across all four models, while persuasiveness remained significant only for GPT-5.6 Sol. Relevant-expert attribution did not produce a universal advantage: credibility was significantly higher for relevant than irrelevant experts for Claude Opus 5.5 and DeepSeek Flash, and Claude Opus 5.5 also showed significantly higher persuasiveness for relevant than irrelevant experts. Exploratory analyses suggested that this pattern may reflect an irrelevant-expertise penalty more than a universal bonus for relevant expertise. No robust evidence showed that relevant expertise disproportionately improved weak arguments. Credibility was descriptively more source-sensitive than logical quality, but corrected direct contrasts were not statistically significant. Overall, LLM evaluation was neither fully source-neutral nor characterized by simple deference to experts. Source expertise produced dimension-specific and model-dependent effects, with credibility showing the clearest sensitivity.

items.title: STEM LECTURERS’ MOTIVATION AS CORRELATES OF TERTIARY INSTITUTIONS OUTPUTS AND RESEARCH INNOVATIONS IN NORTH-CENTRAL NIGERIA
items.abstract: This study examined the relationship between STEM lecturers' motivation, institutional outputs and research innovations in North-Central Nigeria. A correlational survey design was employed. The target population consisted of about 1,840 full-time STEM lecturers in public universities in North-Central Nigeria, from which 368 lecturers were selected using multi-stage sampling technique. Data were collected using the researcher-developed STEM Lecturers' Motivation, Institutional Outputs and Research Innovations Questionnaire (SLMOIRQ). The instrument was validated by experts in Measurement and Evaluation and STEM education and produced a reliability coefficient of 0.82 using Cronbach's Alpha test. Out of 368 distributed questionnaires, 342 were validly returned, giving a 92.9% response rate. Means and standard deviations were used to address the research questions, while Pearson Product-Moment Correlation was used to test the hypotheses at 0.05 significance level. The study found that intrinsic motivation was high (M=3.36, SD=0.64) and was positively related to institutional outputs of good quality (r=0.412, p=0.001). On the contrary, extrinsic motivation was low (M=1.97, SD=0.83) and had weak and insignificant relationship with research innovations (r=0.185, p=0.124). The study concluded that intrinsic motivation is an important correlate of institutional outputs, whereas the current extrinsic motivational conditions are inadequate to significantly stimulate research innovations.

items.title: STRATEGIC PLANNING AND THE ADOPTION OF EMERGING TECHNOLOGIES IN NIGERIAN TELECOMMUNICATION COMPANIES
items.abstract: The rapid evolution of information and communication technologies has significantly transformed the global telecommunications industry, compelling organizations to adopt emerging technologies to remain competitive. This study examines the role of strategic planning in the adoption of emerging technologies in Nigerian telecommunication companies. A survey research design was adopted, targeting managerial and supervisory staff of major telecommunication firms in Nigeria. Based on industry data from the Nigerian Communications Commission (2023), a population of 12,000 employees was identified, from which a sample size of 400 respondents was determined using the Taro Yamane sample size determination formula. Data were collected through structured questionnaires and analyzed using descriptive statistics and the chi-square test of significance. The findings reveal that strategic planning has a significant influence on the adoption of emerging technologies such as 4G, 5G, Internet of Things (IoT), and artificial intelligence within the Nigerian telecommunication sector. The study concludes that effective strategic planning enhances organizational readiness, innovation capacity, and sustained competitive advantage. The paper recommends that telecommunication companies institutionalize comprehensive strategic planning frameworks and that policymakers create supportive environments that encourage technology-driven transformation.

items.title: Structural associations between psychosocial risks and burnout syndrome among mining workers in Peru
items.abstract: Introduction Burnout syndrome is an important occupational-health concern in highly demanding sectors such as mining, where physical, cognitive, and emotional demands coexist with organizational and work–family stressors. The objective of this study was to examine the structural associations between psychosocial risks and burnout syndrome among mining workers in Peru through a path-analysis approach within the structural equation modeling framework. Methods A quantitative, applied, non-experimental, cross-sectional study was conducted with 260 mining workers selected through non-probability purposive sampling. Psychosocial risks were assessed with the SUSESO/ISTAS21 questionnaire and burnout with the Maslach Burnout Inventory. Descriptive analyses and path analysis with 2,000 bootstrap resamples were performed using SPSS and AMOS. Results Psychological demands were positively associated with emotional exhaustion (β = 0.298), whereas active work and skill development was inversely associated with emotional exhaustion (β = −0.429) and depersonalization (β = −0.361). Higher psychosocial-risk scores in social support and leadership quality were positively associated with emotional exhaustion (β = 0.402) and depersonalization (β = 0.441). Depersonalization was positively associated with emotional exhaustion (β = 0.400), and emotional exhaustion was inversely associated with personal accomplishment (β = −0.917). The model accounted for approximately 38% of the variance in depersonalization, 52% in emotional exhaustion, and 66% in personal accomplishment. Discussion The findings support a multidimensional pattern of concurrent associations between psychosocial working conditions and burnout. Because the design was cross-sectional, the coefficients should not be interpreted as causal or temporally ordered effects.

items.title: Super-enhancers: regulatory mechanisms, biological functions, diseases, and therapeutic targets
items.abstract: Super-enhancers (SEs) are operationally defined as clusters of cis-regulatory elements associated with high transcriptional activity and cell-identity genes. They display dense transcription factor and coactivator occupancy, strong H3K27 acetylation, and enhancer-promoter communication, but their annotation varies across platforms, algorithms, and thresholds. This review examines SE architecture, identification, and validation, distinguishing chromatin-based annotation from functional dependence demonstrated by locus-specific perturbations. Mechanisms of SE-associated transcription include pioneer factors, chromatin remodelers, three-dimensional genome organization, transcriptional condensates, non-coding RNAs, and extrachromosomal DNA. Physiological functions in development, immunity, and metabolic homeostasis are considered alongside context-dependent dysregulation in cancer, inflammatory and autoimmune diseases, neurological disorders, and metabolic diseases. Breast cancer provides a model for examining subtype-specific regulation and transcriptional plasticity. Particular attention is given to enhancer remodeling during endocrine therapy, cyclin-dependent kinase 4/6 (CDK4/6) inhibition, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-targeted treatment, and chemotherapy, which may support bypass signaling, stemness, and persistent resistance. Causal regulatory changes must nevertheless be distinguished from correlates of treatment selection. Therapeutic approaches targeting bromodomain and extraterminal domain (BET) proteins, CDK7/9, chromatin regulators, enhancer RNAs, and regulatory loci are critically evaluated. Definitional uncertainty, model dependence, limited reproducibility, systemic toxicity, and insufficient clinical validation remain major barriers. Priorities include standardized annotation, temporally resolved perturbation, single-cell and spatial profiling, artificial intelligence-assisted integration, patient-derived models, and biomarker-guided therapeutic development. Together, these perspectives position SEs as a context-dependent framework linking regulatory architecture to disease progression and treatment resistance, while emphasizing the evidence required to establish therapeutic vulnerabilities.

items.title: Sustaining the Third Pole (Himalayas): Artificial intelligence and blockchain for climate actions
items.abstract: The Himalayas, often known as the 'Third Pole' or 'Water Tower of Asia', are vital for the water security of millions residing in the Asian continent. The region is facing a number of ecological, environmental, and social challenges, such as climate change, biodiversity loss, pollution, and border disputes. Conventional strategies for addressing these challenges have mostly failed to yield satisfactory outcomes. The present study examines the challenges being faced by the Himalayan region. It also explores the potential of AI (Artificial Intelligence) and BT (Blockchain Technology) in solving these challenges by suggesting a conceptual framework for integrating AI and BT to deliver sustainable outcomes in the region. This framework is the multi-stage integration of AI-generated data and BT secure governance mechanism for transboundary climate action. AI offers advanced capabilities for data collection, climate modeling, disaster prediction, and monitoring of biodiversity and ecosystems in the Himalayas. BT can solve the issue of data transparency, security, and trust among the Himalayan nations. However, the implementation of these technologies is constrained due to limited infrastructure, high deployment costs, and cross-border data sharing issues. An inclusive approach leveraging on AI and BT, collaboration between Himalayan nations, support of developed nations, and climate concerns people will be crucial for promoting sustainable development in the Himalayan region.

items.title: Sycophancy as an Asset in LLM Technology: How Model Alignment Breaks Institutional Gatekeeping and Restores Frontline Authority
items.abstract: This paper is part of an independent five-part research series on institutional governance, administrative gatekeeping, and frontline operational practice: Part I: Skynet and HAL 9000: From Science Fiction to Systems Engineering (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23534494) Part II: Commercial Metrics vs. Epistemic Rigour (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23567195) Part III: Automated Confirmation Bias (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23615567) Part IV: Beyond Institutional Risk (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23615568) Part V: Sycophancy as an Asset in LLM Technology (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23886622.) This paper establishes a foundational inversion in how Large Language Models (LLMs) alter the balance of power between entrenched institutions and individual practitioners. While closed institutional deployments of LLMs risk generating automated confirmation bias and epistemic laundering, the intrinsic trait of model sycophancy—long viewed by safety engineers as a severe design defect—functions as a vital asset when harnessed for individual advocacy. By making every effort to support the user's case against the odds, an LLM provides unshakeable psychological safety, non-judgmental iteration, and immediate register translation. Drawing on historical case studies across clinical nursing and skilled manual trades at institutions like Hawker Siddeley, this paper demonstrates how frontline workers can leverage model sycophancy to strip the managerial elite of their linguistic monopoly, bypass credentialist gatekeeping, and project an unyielding, authoritative voice against administrative power. Furthermore, this manuscript is intentionally submitted into formal channels as a methodological Trojan horse—using the structural forms of academic and professional publishing to subvert institutional gatekeeping from within. Keywords: LLM Sycophancy, Institutional Gatekeeping, Frontline Agency, Technical Imperialism, Operational Translation, Systems Safety Engineering, Information Management

items.title: Symbolic-JEPA: Where Symbolic AI Meets Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture for NL–FOL Conversion
items.abstract: Bridging natural language (NL) and formal logic, such as first-order logic (FOL), remains a fundamental challenge for developing trustworthy and explainable artificial intelligence (AI) systems. Despite recent progress, current NL–FOL systems still lack unified semantic–logical representation learning; most adopt late-fusion architectures that loosely couple large language models (LLMs) with symbolic solvers. Furthermore, extended reasoning chains often introduce inefficiencies and lead to violations in logical consistency, structural validity, and formal constraints. In this paper, inspired by Neuro-Symbolic Type-4&5 architectures and the Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA), we propose Symbolic-JEPA , a neuro-symbolic predictive representation model that unifies semantic and logical learning within a single framework. The model incorporates symbolic priors into JEPA, ensuring that the generated FOL expressions remain both semantically faithful and logically consistent. Symbolic-JEPA comprises four key components: a Symbolic Graphizer that unifies NL and FOL inputs into a shared graph space; a Structure-Aware Node & Path Encoder (SANE) that fuses linguistic and structural cues; a Structure-Guided Attention Transformer (SGAT) that injects structure-biased attention; and a Predictor with Micro-Attention that performs clause- and alignment-aware inference efficiently. To support paragraph-level conversion and evaluation, we further introduce ParaLogic , a large-scale NL–FOL dataset with inter-sentence logical annotations (9,344 samples, 28K expressions), along with a three-dimensional evaluation framework spanning parse-, conversion-, and reasoning-level metrics. Experimental results show that Symbolic-JEPA achieves consistently higher logical accuracy, structural well-formedness, and generalization capability compared to neural and LLM-based baselines.

items.title: Symmetry Alignment of User Requirements from Multiple User Groups and Design Elements: Age-Friendly Bathing-Chair Design in Community Eldercare Settings
items.abstract: With the growing demand for community-based eldercare services, bathing safety, caregiving assistance, and facility compatibility in bathing-support spaces have become important issues in age-friendly product design. However, in the design of bathing chairs for community eldercare settings, the alignment of requirements from multiple user groups with design elements from a symmetry perspective remains insufficiently explored. This study investigated six community eldercare service facilities in Hefei, Anhui Province, and developed an integrated research framework integrating multi-stakeholder needs analysis, weight assessment, design-scheme development, and performance validation. User needs were collected through semi-structured interviews, field observations, and questionnaire surveys, and were consolidated into 24 need dimensions using the affinity diagram method. Core needs were then screened using the FKANO model. An evaluation index system comprising six criterion-level dimensions and 19 indicator-level criteria was then established. Integrated weights were calculated using the precedence chart method and the CRITIC method, and the QFD House of Quality was then used to translate the key needs into design elements. The results indicate that bathing-chair design for community-based assisted-bathing settings should prioritize stable support, sit-to-stand assistance, compact storage, lateral access for caregivers, and lockable rotation. Three alternative design schemes were developed based on these results. The TOPSIS evaluation showed that Scheme C achieved the highest relative closeness coefficient of 0.608 and was therefore selected as the preferred alternative. JACK digital human simulation was then used to evaluate its human–product fit and assess the ergonomic suitability of the design. This study provides an integrated design decision-making framework for translating multi-stakeholder needs into specific design elements, thereby offering a systematic methodological basis for bathing-chair design in community eldercare spaces.

items.title: SynForecast artifact
items.abstract: Synthetic time series constitute a substantial share of the training corpora of several recent forecasting foundation models. Existing studies report benefits at small data budgets and modest synthetic proportions, but each evaluates individual combinations of model and generator. Studying these benefits systematically requires generators that support controlled configuration, perturbation, reproducibility and mechanism-level ablation. We review 11 existing generators and find gaps in their combined support for these capabilities. In this paper, we present SynForecast, an open-source Python library that generates synthetic time series from 32 generators, 19 of which implement named mechanisms with a published source in econometrics, quantitative finance, statistical physics and point-process theory. Its design addresses four requirements of forecasting research: (i) output in long format, so that generated data reach a forecasting model without conversion, (ii) perturbations as overlays orthogonal to the generating process, so that a perturbation can be varied while the process is held fixed, (iii) randomness drawn before parallel dispatch, so that output does not depend on the number of workers, and (iv) mechanisms grouped into named families that can be removed one at a time. We evaluate SynForecast on M4 at five frequencies, using a 164K-parameter neural network and a gradient-boosted ensemble. We find that a classical baseline attains the lowest error in nine out of ten frequency-history combinations. Among the learned models, a synthetic prior outperforms the same network trained from scratch at a fixed budget by up to 34% when only a few dozen observations are available. However, it loses to the network trained from scratch at full history at every frequency, and none of the three rescalings of history we pre-specified predicts where the sign changes. At the hourly frequency, where the prior fails at every history, we find that the synthetic corpus lacks daily cycles, and adding them reduces zero-shot error by 43 to 63% for both models. Fine-tuning the pretrained model outperforms training from scratch by up to about 15%, but at short histories a fixed 300-step fine-tune is worse than the pretrained model used as is. Finally, removing the classical family of mechanisms costs about 2% for both models, and three further families have effects of about 1% that replicate on the 20 replicates we ran, but not on the 10 we had pre-specified.

items.abstract: # DESCRIPTION AND KEY ARCHITECTURAL INNOVATIONS ## 1. DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTIONThe disclosed invention relates generally to computational biology, precision oncology, translational medicine, and AI-driven disease model orchestration. More particularly, it provides a disease-agnostic system, architecture, and method for federated multi-modal integration—combining translational multi-omics, electronic health records (EHR), medical and spatial imaging, and white-box gene-regulatory knowledge graphs—governed by zero-raw-data federation (ZRDF) architectures and dynamic self-evolving pipeline orchestration. --- ## 2. KEY ARCHITECTURAL INNOVATIONS * **White-Box Knowledge Graph Governance & LLM Orchestration:** * Replaces black-box inference with mechanistic graph structures (`(:Gene)-[:REGULATES]->(:Pathway)`) interfaced with foundation models. * Governs multi-layer regulatory mechanisms (transcripts, alternative splicing, epigenomics, single-cell/spatial topography) using human-auditable standard operating procedures (SOPs). * **Zero-Raw-Data Federation (ZRDF) Engine:** * Implements a decentralized multi-modal federation framework to synchronize clinical EHR, spatial/medical imaging, and multi-omics across distributed institutions. * Ensures zero raw data exposure by relying exclusively on encrypted embeddings and privacy-preserving model updates. * **Multi-Layer Regulatory Mechanism Modeling & Co-Training:** * Captures intricate regulatory hierarchies spanning genomic variants, chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), differential expression, and alternative splicing isoforms. * Enables simultaneous training and evaluation of foundation models alongside transparent, inspectable graph ontologies. * **Closed-Loop Self-Evolving Orchestration:** * Executes continuous train-test-evaluate orchestration that dynamically refines pipeline hypotheses and knowledge base assertions. * Ingests downstream empirical validation data (such as in vitro PROTAC degradation assays, high-throughput screening, and functional cellular assays) to iteratively re-calibrate edge weights and improve predictive accuracy.

items.title: Talent attraction policies and firm-level AI intensity: evidence from listed firms in China
items.abstract: This paper examines whether talent attraction policies promote firm-level artificial intelligence (AI) intensity. Using panel data on Chinese listed firms from 2005 to 2023, we exploit the staggered adoption of city-level talent attraction policies and estimate a staggered difference-in-differences model. We find that these policies significantly increase AI intensity among firms located in treated cities. Mechanism analysis shows that these policies increase the accumulation of highly educated employees in local firms. Additional evidence on R&D and digital asset investment is consistent with the capital–skill complementarity channel. We also find that urban digital infrastructure strengthens the policy effect. Moreover, analysis by keyword category shows increases in references to AI applications and complementary digital activities in firms’ annual reports. Further analysis shows that the policy effects are stronger in higher-tier and wealthier cities. These findings provide firm-level causal evidence on the role of human capital in AI development and offer policy implications for designing talent policies that support the diffusion of AI technologies.

items.title: Task-Specific Impacts of Cognitive Fatigue on Subjective Experience and Psychomotor Performance
items.abstract: Objective To determine how cognitive fatigue (CF) affects subjective experience and reaction time (RT) performance across tasks with different processing demands (simple, go/no-go, choice), and whether these effects depend on the type of fatigue-inducing mental work. Background CF is a psychobiological state of subjective exhaustion from mental effort that can compromise workplace productivity and safety. Although slowed RT is an often-observed consequence of CF, it is unclear how this compares across RT paradigms and fatigue-inducing tasks. Method Using a remotely administered experiment, 402 participants completed a 60-minute CF (Math-Memory, Stroop, Time Load Dual-Back) or control (documentary) intervention. Subjective ratings (mental fatigue, motivation) and RT performance (simple, go/no-go, choice) were assessed pre- and post-intervention. Results Relative to control, all CF tasks increased subjective fatigue ( p < .001), while motivation declined following Dual-Back and Stroop ( p ≤ .030) but not Math-Memory. Simple and choice RT slowed significantly following all CF interventions vs control ( p < .010), with the greatest choice RT slowing after Stroop ( p ≤ .032). Only Stroop produced significant go/no-go RT slowing ( p = .004). Conclusion Subjective fatigue and simple RT were broadly sensitive to CF, indicating general psychomotor slowing. Conversely, motivation and higher-complexity RT measures showed task-specific effects, perhaps reflecting overlap between fatigue-inducing and RT task demands. Application Task type is important when considering RT as a fatigue assessment tool. These findings support multidimensional (subjective and RT) CF assessments and indicate that simple RT may be effective for rapid, broad fatigue monitoring, whereas complex RT metrics may be useful when exploring task-specific executive processing effects.

items.title: Teacher and Education Leader Perceptions of Digital Competences and Barriers to Digital Transformation of Education
items.abstract: Abstract Digital transformation is reshaping teaching and learning worldwide, yet its benefits remain unevenly distributed and the competences it demands of educators are still contested. This article asks how different educational stakeholders conceptualise the competences required for effective digitalisation of teaching and learning, and what they identify as the principal obstacles to it. The study forms part of an international Erasmus+ Teacher Academy project using a shared interview protocol across partner countries; this article reports the Latvian data. Thirty-two participants - pre-service teachers, in-service teachers and educational leaders, took part in semi-structured interviews, analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Four findings stand out. First, the competences participants named varied systematically with their position in the system: pre-service teachers emphasised operational skills, in-service teachers pedagogical integration, and leaders strategic change management; strikingly few future-oriented competences were technological. Second, language operated as a double constraint, with English proficiency governing access to tools and professional learning while a scarcity of high-quality Latvian-language resources limited classroom use. Third, artificial intelligence was experienced primarily as a challenge to assessment rather than to teaching. Fourth, barriers internal to teachers fear of error and a perceived generational divide, persisted even in well-resourced schools, and change was carried largely by early-adopting colleagues rather than institutional mandate. Together these findings indicate that investment in equipment alone will not deliver digital transformation, and that professional development, resource policy and assessment design need to be addressed as a single problem rather than three separate ones.

items.title: Teachers’ attitudes and behavioural intentions towards AI integration in Chinese higher education: a qualitative interview study
items.abstract: Introduction The rapid expansion of generative AI has intensified scholarly and policy debate over its role in higher education, yet university teachers’ attitudes towards its integration remain complex and context-dependent. This study explores how university teachers perceive, experience, and respond to AI integration in their teaching. Guided primarily by the three-component attitude model and informed by the technology acceptance model and the theory of planned behaviour, the study examines cognitive appraisals, affective responses, behavioural intentions, and perceived support needs. Methods The study draws on semi-structured interviews with 14 university teachers from four higher education institutions in China. The interview data were analysed using codebook-informed thematic analysis combining deductive and inductive coding. Results The findings indicate that teachers generally perceive AI as a supportive rather than substitutive educational tool, valuing it for improving efficiency, supporting lesson preparation, and enriching pedagogical design. Emotional responses varied from enthusiasm and a sense of accomplishment to caution, neutrality, and, in some cases, declining satisfaction. Across the interviews, teachers’ primary concerns centred less on their own replacement than on the perceived risks of inappropriate AI use for students’ independent thinking, reasoning, originality, and authentic understanding. Teachers’ intentions to adopt AI were therefore conditional and bounded, shaped by pedagogical purpose, disciplinary context, student readiness, and the need to maintain teacher control. Teachers also emphasised that sustainable AI integration requires more than general encouragement, calling instead for AI literacy development, discipline-sensitive support, specialised tools, and enabling institutional infrastructure. Discussion Overall, these findings extend contextual understandings of teachers’ AI acceptance by showing how adoption intentions are pedagogically negotiated and highlight the importance of supporting professional judgement and students’ independent thinking in higher education.

items.title: Teachers’ basic psychological need satisfactions and their intentions to use generative artificial intelligence: the mediating role of engagement in professional development
items.abstract: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) offers new opportunities for instructional innovation, yet the psychological mechanisms underlying teachers’ intentions to adopt it remain unclear. Intrinsic motivation is an important internal factor shaping teachers’ intentions to use GenAI and is closely linked to the satisfaction of their basic psychological needs. Drawing on self-determination theory (SDT), this study develops and tests a theoretical framework linking teachers’ basic psychological need satisfaction to their intention to use GenAI through intrinsic motivation and engagement in professional development. Such engagement may foster innovation in GenAI-supported teaching practices. Methods Survey data were collected from 146 teachers participating in a GenAI learning program. Structural equation modeling was used to examine the hypothesized relationships among basic psychological need satisfaction, intrinsic motivation, engagement in professional development, and intention to use GenAI. Results Perceived competence in using GenAI was significantly and positively associated with intrinsic motivation, whereas perceived autonomy and relatedness were not significantly associated with intrinsic motivation. Engagement in professional development mediated the relationship between intrinsic motivation and intention to use GenAI. Discussion These findings provide a nuanced understanding of the psychological mechanisms underlying teachers’ intentions to adopt GenAI, highlighting the roles of perceived competence, intrinsic motivation, and engagement in professional development. They also offer practical implications for supporting the integration of GenAI into teaching.

items.title: Teaching Innovation, Innovating Teaching: Integrating Concept Mapping and GenAI
items.abstract: Management educators face the urgent task of moving students beyond passive consumption to strategic, critical use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI). The goal of this article is to provide a structured framework that transforms GenAI into a tool for cognitive partnership. We present a complete guide for a semester-long, multi-session assignment, designed for undergraduate management education. The assignment’s purpose is to deepen conceptual understanding through experiential learning that combines concept mapping with the critical, comparative use of multiple GenAI tools. Students research a company, build iterative visual knowledge structures, use artificial intelligence (AI) to challenge assumptions, and engage in reflective critical thinking. The teaching focus is on fostering AI literacy and strategic reasoning. This assignment provides instructors with a pedagogically sound method to leverage emerging technologies for active, deep learning in business courses.

items.title: Teaching Writing in the Age of the Chatbot: Automation, Disruption, and the Role of the University
items.abstract: This paper investigates the challenge posed by Large Language Models (LLMs) to teaching and learning how to write at the post-secondary level, situating LLMs as a form of automation affecting both the labour of educators and the labour-markets our students will enter on graduation. The paper argues that the arrival of the chatbot should spur universities to refocus on process-oriented approaches to writing instruction, which foreground the cognitive labour of writing as a practice of thinking. Understanding what writing is – as a practice rather than a product – is critical to understanding the role we should play as university teachers in relation to LLMs as a form of automation that will displace some, but not all, of the capacities that university-level writing practices are meant to cultivate.

items.title: TempCL-Cite: Leveraging Temporal Signals and LLM Positives in Contrastive Learning for Citation Intent Classification
items.abstract: Citation intent classification identifies the underlying functions of scholarly citations and provides semantic information beyond citation counts. However, existing methods pay limited attention to temporal information in citation relationships and are often constrained by the scarcity of high-quality annotated data. To address these challenges, we propose TempCL-Cite, a temporal-aware contrastive learning framework that jointly exploits publication time gaps and large language model (LLM)-generated positive examples. TempCL-Cite encodes the publication time gap and fuses it with textual representations, while using temporal-gap differences together with label differences to guide negative sampling. In addition, a prompt-based LLM generates paraphrases of citation contexts conditioned on their intent labels, providing additional positive views for contrastive learning. The LLM is used only for offline data augmentation and is not required during inference. Experiments on three benchmark datasets show that TempCL-Cite achieves the highest mean Accuracy and Macro-F1 among the compared methods. Ablation results indicate that temporal modeling and contrastive learning contribute to performance in the evaluated settings. Furthermore, temporal-gap-constrained negative sampling outperforms both label-only selection and matched-number random sampling on all three datasets. Comparisons with same-label positives and dropout views show that the proposed LLM-based positive construction strategy achieves the highest mean scores among the evaluated alternatives. BERTScore results indicate strong semantic similarity between the generated and original citation contexts.

items.title: Temporal Evaluation of Hybrid Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Models for Malware Detection using The EMBER Dataset
items.abstract: Malware detection remains a critical challenge in computer science and cybersecurity due to the continuous evolution of malicious software, concept drift, and the declining generalization capability of machine learning models over time. This study investigates the temporal performance of hybrid artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) models for static malware detection using the EMBER dataset. A quantitative experimental design is employed to compare Logistic Regression, Random Forest, LightGBM, and Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) classifiers with a hybrid ensemble approach. The methodology incorporates feature preprocessing, chronological data partitioning, supervised model training, and temporal performance evaluation using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC). Comparative analysis examined differences in classification performance and temporal degradation across the evaluated models. Confusion-matrix analysis and false-negative rates were also considered to assess classification reliability and identify potential detection errors. The hybrid framework combined tree-based learning and neural network predictions to investigate classification performance and detection consistency across temporally distinct malware samples. The significance of this research lies in addressing the limitations of conventional random-split evaluation and providing a more realistic framework for assessing the temporal generalization of intelligent malware detection systems. The findings are intended to inform the development of adaptive, scalable, and robust cybersecurity solutions capable of responding to evolving malware threats.

items.title: TESOL Practitioners’ Perceptions of Using ChatGPT to Design Communicative Tasks for Task-based Language Teaching
items.abstract: Task-based language teaching (TBLT) is increasingly advocated in a range of contexts across the globe as an effective learner-centred and experiential alternative to more traditional teacher-led and instructivist approaches. However, its implementation in classrooms has not always been straightforward. In practice, teachers often struggle not only with understanding what a task is for the purposes of TBLT but also with how tasks fit into the broader learner-centred and experiential pedagogical approach that informs TBLT. Additionally, time constraints and workload pressures have been identified as significant barriers to effective TBLT implementation. In the context of teacher education, this paper considers to what extent ChatGPT as an open access generative artificial intelligence application can support TESOL practitioners with not only generating tasks that are appropriately aligned to TBLT theory but also streamlining the lesson and resource planning and preparation process. The present study investigated what 39 participants in a dedicated postgraduate course focused on TBLT thought of using ChatGPT to design a task, with associated pre-task and post-task activities, for potential classroom use. It draws on data from individual reflective presentations given at the end of the course. Six themes were constructed from a reflexive thematic analysis – three benefits and three limitations of using ChatGPT for task creation purposes. In light of perceived advantages and disadvantages, participants saw using ChatGPT for task generation as a ‘yes … but’ proposition. The findings raise key issues for teachers and teacher educators to be mindful of when using tools like ChatGPT to design tasks.

items.title: The alignment problem is a rate problem: Why waiting for complete governance carries its own risk, and why a deliberate ~ 80% counterweight (NPHE) is a rational response
items.abstract: Proposals for governing artificial intelligence (AI) are often judged by completeness: how much risk they cover before deployment. This paper argues that the alignment problem is also a rate problem. Frontier AI capability, institutional governance capacity, and the supply of high-quality training data change at different rates. Waiting for complete governance before acting therefore carries its own risk, because the gap between capability and governance capacity can widen during the delay. The paper proposes the Nash-Pareto Hybrid Equilibrium (NPHE) as a deliberately incomplete and revisable governance counterweight. NPHE addresses one bounded governance function: real-time regulation of an AI system’s behavioral latitude against a human-ratified setpoint. A threat-weighting function blends defensive and cooperative posture vectors. A critical-integrity override prevents a severe single-axis failure from being averaged away. A bounded discrete proportional-integral-derivative (PID) controller adjusts the blend. The principal contribution is a computable specification of the alignment-error term that the controller requires, with an explicit account of which components are specified, unbuilt, or uncalibrated. NPHE is a conceptual architecture and research agenda, not a validated controller. The estimator, setpoint, and intervention-response dynamics remain unbuilt or unidentified. The controller gains are provisional, and the paper claims no stability proof.

items.title: The Ambient AI Era and Medical Student Education: Insights From Family Medicine Clerkship Directors
items.abstract: Background and Objective: Artificial intelligence (AI) adoption in medicine is rapidly expanding, including ambient AI (AAI), which converts clinician-patient conversations into documentation. Despite growing use among practicing physicians, little is known about student access to AAI or barriers to implementation during medical student clerkships.Methods: We surveyed 174 family medicine clerkship directors (CDs) through the Council of Academic Family Medicine Educational Research Alliance network regarding AAI availability, permissibility, and opinions on student use. We analyzed responses using descriptive statistics and Fisher’s exact tests.Results: Ninety-four CDs responded to AAI-related questions. Student AAI use was permitted for only 3% of core family medicine clerkships. CDs cited missing technology (38.3%) or institutional restrictions (42.5%) as barriers. Opinions on student use were divided: 42.6% opposed any use, 41.5% supported some use, and 16% were unsure. Among those who opposed use, major concerns included potential negative effects on clinical reasoning (82.5%) and communication skills (85%). Supporters of student use were significantly more likely to believe AI will improve training and become commonplace in students’ careers than those who did not support student use of AAI (P<0.0001).Conclusions: Access to AAI for medical students during core family medicine clerkships is rare, and CDs expressed substantial concerns regarding its impact on clinical reasoning and communication skills. Given the expeditious integration of AI into clinical practice, medical educators must be prepared to teach with technology, proactively design curricula that assume AAI availability, and consider modalities in addition to clinical documentation to assess student clinical reasoning.

items.title: The association between interpersonal alienation and problematic use of conversational AI among adolescents: A mediated network analysis of perceived anthropomorphism and AI attachment
items.abstract: Background and aims: With the rapid development of conversational artificial intelligence (CAI), problematic use of conversational AI (PUCAI) among adolescents has attracted increasing attention. However, the underlying psychological factors associated with PUCAI remain unclear. Guided by the Interaction of Person-Affect-Cognition-Execution (I-PACE) model, this study explored the associations between interpersonal alienation, perceived anthropomorphism, AI attachment, and PUCAI. Methods: Data were collected from 1,124 Chinese high school students (516 males, 608 females; Mage = 16.59). Serial mediation analysis and network analysis were conducted. Results: Interpersonal alienation was positively associated with PUCAI. It also had indirect associations through both parallel and serial mediation involving perceived anthropomorphism and AI attachment. Network analysis further revealed that perceived anthropomorphism exhibited the highest bridge expected influence, and emotional trust showed the highest centrality. Conclusion: These findings suggest that adolescent PUCAI is associated not only with general psychological risk factors but also with social-cognitive perceptions and emotional bonding experiences during human-AI interactions. This study provides a novel perspective for understanding problematic use behaviors in emerging human-AI interaction contexts and offers implications for future risk assessment and research on healthy AI use.

items.title: The Effect of AI Absorptive Capacity of Organizations on Workers’ Perceptions About Smart Work Environment Perception Towards Digital Innovation Behavior.
items.abstract: This study investigates the effect of organizational artificial intelligence (AI) absorptive capacity on employees’ perceptions of the smart work environment and how these perceptions influence their digital innovative behavior in the telecommunications industry, with Digital Transformational Leadership as a moderating variable. In this study, two important theoretical perspectives were utilized: Absorptive Capacity Theory, which highlights how organizations acquire, assimilate, and apply their knowledge related to AI, and Socio-Technical Systems Theory, which addresses the connection between technology and the social aspect of the working environment. A quantitative research design was used through partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The data were gathered from 279 respondents working in the telecommunication industry in Jordan. These respondents worked for internet service providers, network operators, and mobile network operators. The findings show that organizational AI absorptive capacity has a strong positive effect on Smart Work Environment Perception (β = 0.742), which in turn enhances Digital Innovative Behavior (β = 0.681). Smart Work Environment Perception partially mediates the relationship between AI absorptive capacity and Digital Innovative Behavior (indirect effect β = 0.506), while Digital Transformational Leadership positively moderates the relationship between AI absorptive capacity and the smart work environment (β = 0.276) and between the smart work environment and Digital Innovative Behavior (β = 0.241). The current research adds value to the literature surrounding AI adoption within organizations by examining how technical capabilities and organizational leadership help foster Digital Innovative Behavior in the telecommunications industry.

items.title: The Effect of Generative AI and Gamification on Enhancing Students’ Motivation Based on the ARCS Model
items.abstract: High school biology learning is often hindered by abstract concepts and cognitive overload, leading to low student motivation. Although generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and gamification show instructional potential, their combined motivational effects remain underexplored. Grounded in the ARCS model, this study examined the impact of integrating ChatGPT-based GenAI and gamification on students’ Attention, Relevance, Confidence, and Satisfaction. A longitudinal quasi-experimental repeated measures design was conducted with 52 high school biology students over eight weeks. Motivation was measured at four time points using a validated ARCS questionnaire and analyzed with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Results showed significant improvements across all ARCS dimensions from pre- to post-intervention (p < .001). Attention and relevance increased steadily, confidence improved in later stages, and satisfaction rose overall. Reported challenges included limited personalized AI feedback, competition-induced anxiety associated with leaderboard-based competition, and increased cognitive load resulting from complex AI-generated content. The findings indicate that GenAI-supported gamification can enhance motivation in biology learning when supported by careful pedagogical design.

items.title: The Effects of Corporate AI Environment Factors on Employees’ Technology Acceptance Attitude and Continuous Intention to Use
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes an imperative survival strategy for modern enterprises, numerous organizations continue to face implementation failures stemming from employees’ psychological resistance. To address the scarcity of empirical research regarding the practical and psychological acceptance of AI in workflows, this study investigates the structural relationships between technological maturity and users’ cognitive adoption. Grounded in an integrated framework utilizing the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), this research conceptualizes the “AI Environment Factor” as a higher-order construct comprising four foundational sub-dimensions: AI System Quality, AI Information Quality, AI Data Quality, and AI Infrastructure. A quantitative survey was administered to 189 corporate practitioners who have utilized enterprise-wide AI systems for at least one year, and the empirical data were analyzed using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM). The analytical results indicate that the AI Environment Factor exerts a statistically significant positive effect on both Perceived Ease of Use and Perceived Usefulness. Furthermore, Perceived Ease of Use was found to positively influence Perceived Usefulness. Ultimately, both Perceived Ease of Use and Perceived Usefulness are significantly associated with the employees’ continuous AI Intention to Use. These findings theoretically contribute to the literature by providing a measurable structural model for the continuance intention phase of organizational AI adoption. Practically, this study offers actionable guidelines for corporate executives, emphasizing that securing rigorous data accuracy and a stable system infrastructure is indispensable for mitigating cognitive load, fostering innovative corporate cultures, and maximizing the efficacy of AI utilization.

items.title: The Evolving Role of Clinical Pharmacists in Pre-, Peri-, and Post-Operative and Critical Care Settings: A Comprehensive Review
items.abstract: Surgery is increasingly recognized as a complex, longitudinal therapeutic process spanning preoperative preparation, anesthesia, intraoperative care, and postoperative recovery rather than an isolated operating room event. Because this continuum is highly medication-intensive and subject to challenges like polypharmacy, rapid drug administration, physiological instability, multiple transitions of care, and communication failures, the perioperative environment carries a high risk for preventable medication errors. This review explores the evolving role of the clinical pharmacist, transitioning from a passive dispenser to an active, multidisciplinary collaborator throughout the surgical pathway. In the preoperative phase, clinical pharmacists improve patient safety by constructing a best possible medication history, clarifying continuation or cessation plans for high-risk home therapies (such as anticoagulants and antidiabetics), and delivering patient education to reduce morning-of-surgery non-adherence. In the intraoperative phase, they support anesthesia providers through system-level and case-level interventions, including the standardization of medication trays and labeling, antimicrobial prophylaxis stewardship, and multimodal analgesic design. Postoperatively, pharmacists collaborate with anesthesiologists to optimize acute pain management, support opioid stewardship, manage thromboembolism prophylaxis, and coordinate comprehensive discharge reconciliation to prevent drug duplication or omission. Collaborative models-such as joint acute pain services and pre-anesthesia consultations-render medication reviews clinically actionable and significantly enhance therapy optimization. Although challenges like staffing constraints, training gaps, and inconsistent clinical integration persist, the future of perioperative pharmacy lies in proactive, technology-enabled care incorporating clinical decision support, barcode administration, and artificial intelligence to solidify clinical pharmacists as core contributors to surgical patient safety.

items.title: The Impact of AI Assistance on the Academic Writing Self-Efficacy of Undergraduates with Different Writing Abilities
items.abstract: Against digital education background, generative AI has become common writing assistance for undergraduates. Existing studies mainly focus on second-language writing and ignore stratified comparisons across learners, while the dual effects of AI on academic writing self-efficacy remain understudied. Based on self-efficacy theory, this paper distributes questionnaires and divides respondents into three proficiency groups by CET-4 scores. Descriptive statistics, group difference tests and correlation analysis are adopted for empirical analysis. The results reveal prevalent AI over-dependence despite its polishing functions. Participants’ writing self-efficacy stays at medium-upper level yet hampered by writing anxiety. AI delivers short-term confidence promotion but impairs independent writing competence in the long run, with stronger influences on low-proficiency students. This stratified dual-path framework offers empirical references for standardized AI application in university writing teaching.

items.title: THE IMPACT OF DIGITAL BANKING AND ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ON PRIVATE BANKING IN SWITZERLAND: ARE CHANGES AHEAD?
items.abstract: Subject of Research. This study focuses on the digital banking landscape and the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in private banking and wealth management in Switzerland. More specifically, it examines how technological innovations – ranging from process automation and generative AI to advanced data analytics – alter the operational dynamics, customer relations, and structural competitiveness of Swiss private banks in the context of shifting client expectations and rigorous regulatory environments. Methodology. The research employs a qualitative analytical research design that uses triangulation of secondary evidence. It systematically integrates and cross-checks academic literature on digital finance, fintech adoption and robo-advisory trust, alongside empirical data, regulatory frameworks and market insights from reputable Swiss and international organisations. The primary data sources analysed were supervisory guides from the Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority (FINMA), reports from the Swiss Bankers Association, digital maturity benchmarks from Deloitte Switzerland and private banking market profitability assessments from KPMG and PwC Switzerland. Purpose. The main objective of this paper is to provide a comprehensive assessment of the impact of digital transformation and the deployment of AI on the traditional Swiss private banking model. By analysing seven key dimensions – technological progress, customer expectations, process optimization, data analytics, risk and security, regulation/compliance, and market trajectories – the study aims to clarify the economic mechanisms driving digital adaptation, identify the structural barriers preventing rapid technology adoption, and evaluate the strategic options available to Swiss banks facing intense global competition and margin compression. Findings and Conclusion. The study reveals a significant discrepancy between Switzerland's position as a global leader in asset management, with CHF 9.3 trillion under management, and its digital banking maturity score of 39 out of 60. Although private banking clients continue to establish relationships based on traditional factors such as reputation, trust and personal referrals, they are also demanding friction-free digital execution, personalised dashboards and virtual investment simulations. AI has been proven to have high economic value when acting as a productivity layer centred around advisors, optimising processes such as client onboarding, document extraction, compliance screening and portfolio monitoring. However, it is not as effective when acting as an autonomous replacement for human relationship managers. Ultimately, the integration of digital banking and AI is causing a clear market polarisation. Large-scale institutions are successfully absorbing the substantial fixed costs associated with technology, data governance and regulatory compliance under the frameworks of FINMA and the European Union (such as DORA and the EU AI Act). Conversely, smaller Swiss private banks are under severe pressure to increase their profitability and consolidate, unless they adopt highly focused niche advisory models. The paper therefore concludes that urgent regulatory attention and strategic repositioning are necessary to preserve the overall image and international attractiveness of the Swiss private banking ecosystem.

items.title: The Influence of Employees' Integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence Tools on Organizational Data Exposure Risks Within the Context of Data Security Posture in Uganda
items.abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, and Claude into everyday work practices has created a new and poorly governed channel through which organizational data can leave the enterprise. This review synthesized theoretical, empirical, and practitioner literature on the relationship between employees' integration of GenAI tools and organizational data exposure risks, situating that relationship within the broader context of organizational data security posture. The review is organized around four themes, the extent, drivers, and patterns of employee GenAI integration in the workplace, the phenomenon of "Shadow AI" and "Bring Your Own AI" (BYOAI), the mechanisms through which GenAI use generates data exposure, leakage, and compliance risks, and the role of data security posture encompassing governance frameworks, visibility, policy, and employee security behavior in moderating those risks. Literature from developed economies dominates the field, while evidence from Uganda and the wider Sub-Saharan African context remains scarce. The review identifies key theoretical anchors (the Technology Acceptance Model, Protection Motivation Theory, and information security governance perspectives), synthesized documented incidents such as the Samsung ChatGPT data leak, and highlights empirical survey evidence showing widespread unsanctioned use of GenAI by employees. It concludes by delineating conceptual and empirical gaps particularly the absence of studies that jointly model GenAI integration, data exposure risk, and data security posture in developing country organizational settings and proposes a conceptual framework to guide future research in Ugandan organizations.

items.title: The Influence of Smart Home Appliance Technology Perception on Sustainable Consumption Behavior: The Serial Mediating Effects of Perceived Value and Perceived Consumer Effectiveness Within the SOR Framework
items.abstract: Against the backdrop of the digital economy, the deep integration of artificial intelligence and Internet of Things technologies has driven the rapid adoption of smart home appliances, providing new pathways for energy conservation, emissions reduction, and sustainable consumption in households. However, the psychological mechanisms underlying the transformation of smart home appliance technology perceptions into sustainable consumption behaviors—particularly the serial mediating roles of perceived value and perceived consumer effectiveness—remain to be thoroughly investigated. Based on the SOR theory, a research model was constructed with perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use as stimulus variables, perceived value and perceived consumer effectiveness as organism variables, and sustainable consumption behavior as the response variable. Empirical analysis was conducted using SmartPLS based on 508 valid questionnaires. The results indicate that the model exhibits good explanatory power (R2 = 50.4%), with significant positive relationships among all variables. Among these, perceived usefulness has a positive association with perceived value; perceived value is significantly associated with perceived consumer effectiveness; and perceived consumer effectiveness has a significant direct association with sustainable consumption behavior. Furthermore, perceived value and perceived consumer effectiveness play significant mediating and serial mediating roles. This study reveals the psychological transmission mechanism through which the perceived technology of smart home appliances influences sustainable consumption behavior, expands the application of SOR theory, and provides a theoretical basis and practical guidance for smart home appliance companies to formulate green marketing strategies oriented toward value enhancement and efficacy strengthening.

items.title: The library of the future: Services, agility and a functional identity continuum
items.abstract: Abstract Academic libraries are currently undergoing fundamental change. Digitisation, open access, research data management, artificial intelligence, changing learning and research practices, and the transformation of the publishing system are broadening their remit whilst simultaneously raising users’ expectations of them. In international professional discourse, this development is often described as a transition from a collection-centred library to one that is more service- and workflow-oriented. (Dempsey and Malpas 2018; Pinfield, Cox and Rutter 2017; Lavoie and Bryant 2026) This brings with it new opportunities. Libraries can develop new services, align themselves more closely with research and learning processes, and expand their role as an infrastructure for academic communication. At the same time, an institutional tension is emerging. Library services are increasingly breaking down into individual services, some of which could also be provided by other organisational units. This makes the question of what enables the library to remain recognisable as a library all the more pressing. This article proposes framing this question using the concept of the ‘functional identity continuum’. This does not imply a static adherence to traditional forms, but rather an interconnection between collection, selection, cataloguing, contextualisation, access, space, preservation, outreach and institutional responsibility. From this perspective, the library of the future remains a plausible institutional form only if it sustainably integrates new services and anchors them to a core library function.

items.title: The mediating role of self-efficacy in the relationships of technophilia and positive emotional experience with perceived learning effectiveness in AI-supported EFL education
items.abstract: Abstract Despite the increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into English as a Foreign Language (EFL) education, the psychological mechanisms linking learners’ technological dispositions and emotional experiences to perceived learning effectiveness remain undertheorized and empirically underexplored. This study examined whether self-efficacy served as a statistical mediator in the relationships of technophilia and positive emotional experience with perceived learning effectiveness in AI-supported EFL education. A cross-sectional survey was conducted involving 234 students enrolled in English-language courses at a private college of health sciences. Adapted multi-item scales on technophilia, positive emotional experience, self-efficacy, and perceived learning effectiveness were administered. Structural equation modeling with bootstrapping (5000 resamples) was used to examine direct and indirect associations. Self-efficacy demonstrated the strongest direct association with perceived learning effectiveness (β = 0.375, p = 0.001). Positive emotional experience was strongly associated with self-efficacy (β = 0.624, p < 0.001), and its indirect association with perceived learning effectiveness through self-efficacy was significant (β = 0.234, 95% CI [0.128, 0.351]). Technophilia was also positively associated with self-efficacy (β = 0.307, p = 0.002), and its indirect association with perceived learning effectiveness through self-efficacy was significant. The findings were consistent with self-efficacy partially mediating both relationships. These findings suggest that learners’ confidence in managing AI-supported tasks plays an important role in linking affective dispositions to perceived effectiveness appraisals. The study contributes to computer-assisted language learning (CALL) research by clarifying how positive orientation toward AI-supported technologies, emotional experience, and efficacy beliefs jointly relate to learners’ perceptions of effective AI-supported language learning. Pedagogically, the findings suggest that progressively scaffolded practice and mastery-oriented AI tasks may strengthen self-efficacy and improve learners’ perceived effectiveness in AI-supported EFL environments.

items.title: The ovarian cellular ecosystem in polycystic ovary syndrome: from cellular heterogeneity to clinical relevance
items.abstract: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is one of the most biologically heterogeneous disorders in reproductive endocrinology, extending far beyond the classical features of hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction, and polycystic ovarian morphology. Although substantial progress has been made in defining the endocrine, metabolic, genetic, epigenetic, and inflammatory mechanisms associated with PCOS, these processes have largely been investigated independently, and their contribution to the marked clinical and biological heterogeneity of the disorder remains incompletely understood. Recent advances in cellular-resolution biology, including single-cell and single-nucleus transcriptomics, spatial omics, and multimodal molecular profiling, together with computational systems biology, enable increasingly detailed characterization of cellular states, spatial organization, and molecular relationships within the ovarian-follicular environment. In this Review, we use the ovarian cellular ecosystem as an operational systems framework to test whether PCOS-associated abnormalities observed in individual ovarian and follicular compartments form reproducible higher-order patterns of multicellular organization. The framework is organized across five measurable domains: cellular composition and states, intercellular signaling relationships, spatial niche organization, cross-compartment molecular coupling, and systemic-ovarian coupling. Current direct human cellular-resolution evidence remains sparse and compartment-specific. Available studies support altered molecular and cellular states within selected ovarian and follicular compartments more strongly than coordinated, spatially organized, or progressive ecosystem-wide remodeling. We critically evaluate how cellular-resolution, spatial, multi-omics, computational and artificial intelligence approaches can be used to test these ecosystem-level hypotheses, explicitly distinguishing direct measurement from computational inference and identifying the validation required for functional or causal interpretation. Finally, we discuss the translational implications of this framework for biologically informed patient stratification, ecosystem-derived biomarker discovery, mechanism-informed therapeutic development, and precision reproductive endocrinology. By integrating current evidence within a falsifiable framework, this Review defines measurable features and validation criteria for testing ovarian ecosystem organization in PCOS and identifies the critical evidence gaps that future cellular-resolution, spatial, and multi-omic studies must address. This provides a practical roadmap for determining whether reproducible ovarian ecosystem states can improve biological stratification, biomarker discovery, or therapeutic target identification beyond compartment-specific abnormalities and established systemic and clinical determinants.
